## Abstract
On March 24, 1976, the Armed Forces in Argentina overthrew the constitutional government led by María Estela Martínez de Perón and established a military dictatorship over the country. Over the next few years, the government ran a systematic campaign of forced disappearance in which thousands of people were taken to clandestine detention centers (CCDs) spread across the country. This project will use spatial point pattern analysis to investigate whether the locations of these centers simply tracked where people lived, or whether they reflect where the government saw political threats based on the political ideology of an area, or something else. 

The main dataset is the 2014 Registro Unificado de Victimas del Terrorismo del Estado (RUVTE) registry of CCDs, compiled by Argentina's Ministry of Justice and Human Rights. It contains 676 sites with latitude and longitude, of which 624 are marked as corroborated. For political ideology, the data comes from Lupu & Stokes' 2009 paper "The Social Bases of Political Parties in Argentina, 1912-2003" which has data on election results by departamento (similar to a US county) over time. I also have data from the RUVTE on the victims themselves, however, precise locations of disappearances are not known so this data would be aggregated at the departamento level. 

To start, I will focus on the greater Buenos Aires area which has 52 CCDs, and then, if time allows, expand to other provinces like Tucuman, which has an unusually high concentration of centers. I will map CCD locations and compute global and local Moran’s I on departamento-level CCD rates per capita. For the formal test, I will estimate the intensity function under a null model in which CCD intensity depends only on population density. I will run 999 Monte Carlo simulations of that model and compare the observed intensity and the inhomogeneous pair correlation function against the simulation. Then, I will add the political covariates to see whether they account for the remaining structure. Victim data can potentially be used to check whether centers and victims are distributed alike.

This analysis will have several limitations. The registry likely undercounts sites, and discovery may be biased toward areas with more survivor testimony. Many CCDs operated inside pre-existing police and military facilities, so their locations may reflect existing infrastructure rather than deliberate placement. Also, the most recent electoral data predates the dictatorship (1973), and Peronist vote share is an imperfect proxy for ideology given the movement’s internal divisions.

On March 24, 1976, the Armed Forces in Argentina overthrew the constitutional government led by María Estela Martínez de Perón and established a military dictatorship over the country (Aguila, 2023). In the years leading up to the coup, political violence increased due to a combination of armed conflict, state-sanctioned repression, and an economic crisis. Leftist guerrilla groups were carrying out armed attacks, the government had authorized the military to “annihilate subversion” throughout the country, and a failed economic adjustment in 1975 had triggered rising inflation and a recession (Águila, 2023; Marongiu, 2006). By the time the armed forces took power, the government had almost no public support or political legitimacy, and there was little to no resistance to the coup (Águila, 2023). Many Argentines initially received the coup with a sense of relief. After years of political violence and economic instability, broad sectors of society, particularly the middle classes, viewed military rule as a response to their demand for order and stability. Popular magazines reinforced this view by framing the coup as a “necessary” solution to the political crisis and portraying guerrilla violence as a threat to society as a whole (Gomes & Robertini, 2026). Behind this image of order, however, the junta carried out a campaign of clandestine repression against anyone it considered "subversive," kidnapping people, holding and torturing them in secret detention centers, and refusing to acknowledge that they had ever been detained (Calveiro, 1998). Over time, this support eroded. Mothers of the disappeared began publicly demanding information about their children, the economy fell into another severe crisis, and Argentina’s defeat by the United Kingdom in the 1982 Malvinas (Falklands) War destroyed what remained of the regime’s legitimacy, forcing it to call elections and return power to a civilian government in December 1983 (Franco, 2018). After the return to democracy, the new government created the National Commission on the Disappearance of Persons (CONADEP) to investigate the fate of the disappeared, and its work, along with that of later state registries, has made it possible to identify and locate hundreds of the detention centers used during the dictatorship (CONADEP, 1986; RUVTE, n.d.).
